The Outer Space Treaty has been in effect for 53 years. Although the wording of it is very broad, and the articles often very unspecific, it has served as the legal framework for international activities in space. Since its inception, space has been peaceful, and the treaty has served to stop the militarisation of space. Space is already dangerous enough without war - coincidentally, NASA's first fatality in space occured during the Apollo 1 mission, which occurred on January 27, 1967, the day the Outer Space Treaty was signed by the US, Russia and the UK.

The amendment we would like to propose relates to the use or existence of weapons in space. The treaty already contains an article which outlaws the use of nuclear, chemical and biological weaponry in space, but it does not specify anything about conventional or kinetic weapons. It is not a threat that is imminent, but one that should be considered, as the legal framework concerning space related activities is still very young.

To date, there have been a few conventional and kinetic weapons in space. Russia tested [potential nuclear/kinetic bombardment systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fractional_Orbital_Bombardment_System), and has equipped [space stations with conventional weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz#Defense_measures). They also provide astronauts with small arms for the purpose of defending themselves if they land in a dangerous area upon re-entry.

We are proposing a ban on conventional and kinetic weapons in space. This ban will not apply to small arms given to astronauts for the intent of protecting themselves when they come back to Earth, but it will apply to the use of them in space.

This is our proposed definition of conventional weapons:

*"Weapons that include, but are not necessarily limited to: weapons that are in wide use that are not weapons of mass destruction. Arms used in conflicts or wars, such as small arms, light weapons, bombs, mines, shells and cluster munitions. Rockets and missiles that do not have the purpose of transportation, exploration or of scientific testing. Any weapons that are regulated by the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, the Convention on Cluster Munitions, The Ottawa Treaty and the Arms Trade Treaty."*

We are also proposing a ban on kinetic weapons. Due to kinetic weapons being so difficult to define, (particularly as it is very easy to define spacecraft as kinetic weapons, though that was not their purpose upon construction) we are requesting input from all nations affected by the proposed amendment to this treaty.

China frowns on any tampering with the OST, and plans to invoke its Article XVI right to withdraw from the Treaty if it this proposal is ratified.

The UK would like to remind China that this will gravely affect relations with other nations, not just with regards to co-operation in space, but here on Earth. If China was to withdraw from the treaty, Article II would not apply, meaning China could claim objects in space. Article IV, pertaining to the placement or use of nuclear weapons in space would also not apply, which would be a concern to many countries, particularly the US. Not only this, but military bases and weapons testing amongst other things could be conducted in space.

Perhaps the most important from a Chinese point of view may be Article V:

States Parties to the Treaty shall regard astronauts as envoys of mankind in outer space and shall render to them all possible assistance in the event of accident, distress, or emergency landing on the territory of another State Party or on the high seas. When astronauts make such a landing, they shall be safely and promptly returned to the State of registry of their space vehicle.

In carrying on activities in outer space and on celestial bodies, the astronauts of one State Party shall render all possible assistance to the astronauts of other States Parties.

States Parties to the Treaty shall immediately inform the other States Parties to the Treaty or the Secretary-General of the United Nations of any phenomena they discover in outer space, including the moon and other celestial bodies, which could constitute a danger to the life or health of astronauts.

This would essentially mean that China would not be liable for the well-being of astronauts from other nations, which would make it extremely difficult for China to conduct missions in space with other nations, as they would not want to risk dealing with a country that was not bound by international law to abide by the principle of absolute co-operation in space, as outlined in the article.

Additionally, China would not be liable for damages to other countries as a result of debris falling from space. The Secretary-General of the United Nations would not have to be informed of activities in space conducted by the Chinese government - or by independent agencies within China, the actions of which you would also not be responsible for if Article VI no longer applied. You would also not retain ownership of objects launched into space, as specified under Article VIII, meaning anything taken from you in space would not be a violation of the treaty as you are not a party of it.

In conclusion, withdrawing from this treaty would not just be a bad thing for the international community, but for China. However, if China is not willing to agree to an amendment regarding conventional and kinetic weapons in space, the reasons behind such a decision still being uncertain to us, we recommend that you simply not accept the amendment instead.
